EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  

==============================================================  

1. Identification Strategy  
--------------------------------------------------------------  
Primary strategy: stacked difference-in-differences (DID) with an event-study dimension, implemented at the monthly HS-10-by-origin-country (import side) and HS-10-by-destination-country (export side) level.

Why it fits:  
•  The tariff shocks were discrete, date-stamped and applied only to a subset of product–country pairs, leaving a large set of unaffected pairs that can serve as contemporaneous controls.  
•  The panel is rich (≈3.5 million obs. = 12,000 products × ≈30 countries × 36 months), allowing for high-dimensional fixed effects that soak up most confounding demand and supply shocks.  
•  The timing was exogenous to individual products’ pre-2018 monthly fluctuations (tariffs were driven by macro-political motives, not by any single HS-10’s performance).  
•  A stacked DID/event-study permits (i) testing for pre-trends, (ii) estimating dynamic effects, and (iii) exploiting multiple waves (solar/washers, steel/aluminum, four Section 301 rounds).  
Secondary strategy: shift-share (“Bartik”) DID at the county × month level to measure distributional welfare effects. Counties’ ex-ante employment composition provides quasi-random exposure to the tariff schedule.

2. Treatment and Control  
--------------------------------------------------------------  
Unit of observation (imports): i = HS-10 product p imported from origin country o in month t.  
Unit of observation (exports): i = HS-10 product p exported to destination country d in month t.

2.1 Treatment variable  
Import side:  
Treat_{pot} = 1 if product p imported from country o is subject to a new statutory U.S. tariff at rate τ>0 that first becomes effective in month T_{po} ∈ 2018:2–2019:9; 0 otherwise.  
Export side:  
Retaliation_{pdt} = 1 if product p exported to country d is hit by a retaliatory tariff that first takes effect in month R_{pd}.  

Continuous intensity measure: Δτ_{po} or Δτ_{pd} (percentage-point change). Main specs scale outcomes by Δτ (“dose–response” DID).

2.2 Control group  
For imports: product–country pairs that (i) never receive a tariff during 2017:1–2019:4 or (ii) receive it in a later wave and therefore serve as controls until their own treatment date (stacked DID).  
For exports: analogous definition using retaliation timing.

2.3 Treatment timing  
Event date 0 = first month the new tariff is collected (lag U.S. tariff schedules by one month to ensure shipments clear customs). Leads k = −12,…,−1 test parallel trends; lags k = 0,…, +18 trace dynamics.

No running variable → not an RDD.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
--------------------------------------------------------------  
A1 Parallel trends: In absence of tariffs, treated and control varieties would have evolved similarly after 2018. Plausible because assignment was driven by macro-political motives and because we include rich fixed effects.  
A2 No anticipation: Firms could not perfectly foresee tariffs six months ahead; pre-filings became public only weeks before implementation. We will test for anticipatory effects with event-study leads.  
A3 Stable unit treatment value (SUTVA): Tariffs on i do not directly affect outcome of j≠i. Some substitution across origins is possible; we address with origin-by-product fixed effects and by estimating diversion effects separately.  
A4 Exogeneity of exposure in county shift-share: Counties’ 2016 employment mix is predetermined relative to 2018 tariffs; labor reallocation across sectors is slow at an annual horizon.  
A5 No major concurrent policy differentially hitting treated varieties (e.g., simultaneous antidumping duties). We control for other trade remedies using AD/CVD databases.

4. Threats to Identification & Remedies  
--------------------------------------------------------------  
T1 Substitution/Trade diversion: Importers may switch origins within an HS-10 to avoid tariffs, violating SUTVA. Remedy: (i) include origin-invariant product fixed effects to net out demand shifts; (ii) estimate cross-origin elasticities to quantify diversion, treating them as outcome of interest rather than bias.  
T2 Differential commodity price shocks (e.g., soybean price collapse in 2018) coincide with China’s retaliation. Remedy: control for world commodity prices at HS2 × month level; include destination-specific month fixed effects in export regressions.  
T3 Selection of retaliation list correlated with past growth of U.S. exports (reverse causality). Remedy: placebo test using lists that were floated in April 2018 but never implemented; test pre-period growth differentials.

5. R Code Outline  
--------------------------------------------------------------  
```r
# 0. Packages --------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast data handling
library(fixest)       # high-dim FE and clustering
library(lubridate)
library(metRology)    # for delta method in welfare calcs

# 1. Data loading ----------------------------------------------------------
imp  <- fread("us_imports_hs10_country_month.csv")     # values, quantities, duties
exp  <- fread("us_exports_hs10_country_month.csv")
tar  <- fread("us_treat_tariff_schedule.csv")          # HS10-country, eff_date, dTariff
ret  <- fread("retaliation_schedule.csv")              # HS6-country, eff_date, dTariff
cbp  <- fread("county_sector_emp_2016.csv")            # for county shift-share

# 2. Variable construction -------------------------------------------------
# Merge tariffs onto trade panel
imp <- merge(imp, tar, by = c("hs10","origin_country"), all.x = TRUE)
exp <- merge(exp, ret, by.x = c("hs10","dest_country"), 
             by.y = c("hs6_matched","country"), all.x = TRUE)  # expand HS6 to HS10

# Replace NA with 0
imp[is.na(dTariff), dTariff := 0]
exp[is.na(dTariff), dTariff := 0]

# Event time
imp[, treat_date := as.Date(eff_date)]
imp[, event_time := as.numeric(month(date) + 12*year(date) - 
                               (month(treat_date)+12*year(treat_date)))]
exp[, event_time := ... ]  # analogous

# Treatment dummies
imp[, treated := dTariff>0]
imp[, post := (date >= treat_date)]
imp[, dose := dTariff]     # continuous intensity

# Outcomes
imp[, ln_qty := log(quantity+1)]
imp[, ln_val := log(value+1)]
imp[, unit_price := log(value/quantity)]

# 3. Main DID/Event-study specification ------------------------------------
# Model: y_{pot} = Σ_{k=-12}^{+18} β_k * 1[event_time==k]*treated + γ_po + γ_t + ε
lead_lag <- paste0("i(event_time, treated, ref = -1)")
fml <- as.formula(paste("ln_qty ~", lead_lag, "| hs10_origin + month + 0"))
est_qty <- feols(fml, data = imp[event_time >= -12 & event_time <= 18], 
                 cluster = ~hs10_origin)

# Continuous (dose) DID
est_dose <- feols(ln_qty ~ dose*post | hs10_origin + month, data = imp, 
                  cluster = ~hs10_origin)

# 4. County shift-share analysis ------------------------------------------
# Construct county-level tariff exposure
# Exposure_c,t = Σ_s (Employment_c,s2016 / totEmp_c) * avg Δτ_s,t
sector_tau <- imp[, .(avg_dTariff = weighted.mean(dTariff, quantity)), 
                  by = .(naics4, date)]
cbp <- merge(cbp, sector_tau, by = "naics4", allow.cartesian=TRUE)
cbp[, weight := emp2016 / sum(emp2016), by = county]
cbp[, expo := sum(weight * avg_dTariff), by = .(county, date)]

county_outcome <- feols(log(real_income) ~ expo | county + month, 
                        data = county_panel, cluster = ~state)

# 5. Robustness check: placebo with pre-announced but never-implemented list
imp[, placebo := (hs10 %in% unimplemented_list)]
placebo_est <- feols(ln_qty ~ placebo*post | hs10_origin + month, 
                     data = imp[date <= as.Date("2018-12-31")], 
                     cluster = ~hs10_origin)
```

6. Expected Results  
--------------------------------------------------------------  
Theory (Armington + standard import demand) predicts a price elasticity near −2. Short-run pass-through of tariffs to importer prices ≈ 100 % (i.e., border prices rise one-for-one). Therefore:  
•  Import quantities of treated varieties fall roughly 20–40 % when facing a 25 pp tariff.  
•  Border prices rise by ≈25 %, retail prices by ≈10–15 % once partial pass-through and substitution are considered.  
•  U.S. aggregate real income falls modestly (≈0.03–0.06 % of GDP in 2019Q4), while farm counties in the Midwest/Southwest experience welfare losses of −0.3 % personal income; steel-intensive Great-Lakes counties gain slightly.  
•  Tariffs and retaliation disproportionately target counties with higher 2016 Trump vote shares, especially retaliation (politically motivated by partners).

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment  
--------------------------------------------------------------  
(DID checklist of Angrist & Pischke, scored 1 = yes, 0 = maybe/no)

C1 Parallel trends visually supported by pre-period event-study coefficients: 1  
C2 No anticipation or timing manipulation: 0.5  
C3 No spillovers/SUTVA across units: 0.5  
C4 Correct functional form & standard errors (FE + clustering): 1  
C5 Robustness to alternative specifications (placebo, dose-response, export diversion): 1  

Total ≈ 4/5.
